entry.title: A First-Hour Playbook for a Refrigeration Controller Alert
entry.summary:
A First-Hour Playbook for a Refrigeration Controller Alert
Most security teams have a playbook for a compromised server and none for a compromised refrigerator. The CERT-FR alert shows what the first hours look like when the assets are cold-chain controllers, and the sequence differs from a typical host incident. Before isolating anything, establish what the site actually runs. A controller family from Danfoss, Copeland or Dixell, with a model and firmware version, is the minimum. CERT-FR's alert names AK-SM and AK-SC on the Danfoss side and XWEB on the Copeland and Dixell side. CERT-FR advised operators to take affected controllers off the internet and restore remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. The agency also said filtering connections by IP address is acceptable only as a temporary emergency measure. The reported behaviour was control-mode manipulation rather than data theft. According to Le Monde, attackers kept some units in defrost mode for up to eight hours, which delayed alarms. Review controller logs for mode changes outside the site's schedule, silenced alarms, and configuration edits that widened thresholds. A factory reset is not remediation for an exposed end-of-life device. CERT-FR states that the device will remain vulnerable and is likely to be compromised again if it stays exposed. Replacement or permanent network isolation are the real fixes. title="StoreView Web" on 21 October 2026 returned 271 assets globally, 55 in France, and smaller counts in the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium. Every step above is a network or process control, not a signature. That is what makes it usable before attribution is settled. CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012: https://cert.cyber.gouv.fr/alerte/CERTFR-2026-ALE-012/
SecurityWeek, supermarket refrigeration attack coverage: https://www.securityweek.com/supermarket-refrigeration-attack-widens-to-copeland-dixell-controllers/

entry.title: SMS OTP Delivery Failure Budget (Carrier Filtering on Shared Routes)
entry.summary: Route a healthtech contact form only after the phone challenge reaches a terminal result, and preserve the form while it does. SMS OTP delivery can fail for ordinary reasons: an unregistered sender, carrier filtering, a handset problem, or a temporary routing delay. The useful design is a recoverable queue, not an optimistic send() call followed by a timer. My decision rule is blunt: delivery reliability beats integration polish. Register the sender for the launch markets, poll delivery state, rate-limit resends, and keep a separately engineered fallback. An accepted API request is not proof that a code appeared on the patient's phone. entry.title: Whitelist, not blacklist: why a launch bot should buy only what passes
entry.summary: Many open-source sniper and copy bots filter the same way: fetch the new launch, run a few checks, and skip it if something looks bad. Mint authority still active, skip. Creator rugged before, skip. Otherwise, buy. That is a blacklist. It feels safe because every rule you add removes a known bad case. The problem is the base rate. When most launches fail, removing the obviously bad ones barely moves the odds of the ones you keep. The alternative is a whitelist: buy only when every check positively passes, and treat anything else (a warning, a missing answer, a timeout) as "no". This post shows the difference on real numbers, then gives you a gate you can drop into a bot and a script to measure your own filter. entry.summary: Most teams check an LLM-assisted decision system for fairness by comparing approval rates across groups.
